strengths: DDOME addresses a useful problem: personalizing predictions for unseen federated clients without labeled adaptation data. Selecting a small client-specific expert subset and then routing individual samples provides a practical mechanism.

Experiments cover four image and text datasets, with promising reported gains, including 78.6% on CIFAR100 and 74.9% on Yahoo! Answers. Ablations investigate pretrained-model quality, anchor sampling, initialization, overlapping label distributions, and changing client populations.

The algorithm, training losses, and communication protocol are reasonably clear. The candid discussion of pretrained-model dependence, communication overhead, limited scalability, and fairness risks is valuable.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false under the stated Gaussian scaling. Take m=2 with mutually orthogonal ground-truth router and expert vectors. For x~N(0,I/sqrt(d)), E[y²]=1/sqrt(d), so zero experts achieve loss 1/(2sqrt(d)). The two exact minimization stages cannot increase this bound, contradicting the claimed dimension-independent Ω(1) loss. Appendix J additionally changes the covariance to I/d and applies a random-subspace bound to span(V,V*) without controlling its overlap with W*; W*=V* is permitted by the theorem. These are substantive correctness problems.

The claimed necessity of joint training exceeds the analysis even independently of those errors. The theorem examines only one experts-first schedule with initially random, frozen routing. Failure of that schedule would not exclude other sequential or alternating procedures. There is also no controlled joint-versus-sequential experiment connecting the theoretical claim to DDOME.

The main specialization experiments supply substantial structure explicitly: Appendix A constructs anchor clients from disjoint label groups, assigns each to a fixed expert, and trains the router against those assignments. Thus, the results do not establish the broad claim of discovering specialization without explicit task structure. The overlapping-label experiments help, but anchor-free performance is substantially weaker, and independently trained anchor experts followed by router training are not evaluated.

The headline improvements require stronger baseline validation. In Table 1, a frozen common expert already achieves 93% on CIFAR10, compared with 95.7% for DDOME and 58.4% for FedAvg. Several other baselines also deteriorate severely from initialization. Competitive validation-based tuning and frozen-feature classifier baselines are needed to distinguish specialization benefits from avoiding baseline degradation; text experiments additionally use different optimization schedules for DDOME.

Capacity and efficiency comparisons remain incomplete. Main experiments use 5–10 experts for DDOME versus two for FedMix. Appendix G partially addresses matched capacity, but only in a limited setting. No end-to-end accuracy-versus-communication or computation measurements account for common-model inference, feature storage, and expert training, so broad resource-efficiency claims remain insufficiently supported.

Reproducibility and statistical reliability are limited by missing pretrained-checkpoint provenance and training details, exact router dimensions, comprehensive tuning protocols, and repeated-run statistics. Tables 4, 7, and 8 report best test accuracy across rounds without a stated independent validation procedure, creating a risk of optimistic model selection.

Originality is insufficiently established relative to existing joint MoE training and mixture-based personalized federated learning, including FedEM. Appendix I's K-means visualization does not justify dismissing approaches that explicitly model mixed client distributions. A more precise comparison is needed to identify the contribution beyond combining pretrained features, sparse routing, and anchor supervision.
